passage:
Rafiq: street flooded again. third year. the councillor doesn't care
Rafiq: this guy on that channel says it's all because of them. honestly he's the only one who's angry about it
Joseph: I'm angry about it too
Joseph: but "them" who? the rain?
Rafiq: you know what I mean
Joseph: I do. that's why I'm asking
Joseph: the youth group is clearing drains on Saturday. and Councillor Bhatia has open hours at 11
Joseph: she actually listened when we went about the streetlight last year. it got fixed
Rafiq: one streetlight
Joseph: one more than the channel fixed
Rafiq: ok that's fair
Joseph: come for drains, then we'll go together. bring the photos from 2023 and 2024
Rafiq: I have videos from every year
Joseph: perfect. that's evidence, not just anger
Rafiq: fine. 8 am?
Joseph: 8 am. bring gloves

qa.q: What is the youth group doing on Saturday?
qa.a: The youth group is clearing drains on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's first message reveal about the channel's appeal?
qa.a: Rafiq feels ignored after three years of flooding, and the channel appeals because it seems to be the only voice sharing his anger.

qa.q: What makes Joseph's suggestions a good way forward?
qa.a: Joseph takes the anger seriously, then offers real action, clearing drains, and a meeting with a councillor who has listened before, using Rafiq's videos as evidence.

qa.q: How might Joseph see the channel's message differently from Rafiq?
qa.a: Joseph shares the anger but sees that blaming "them" fixes nothing, while the streetlight shows what action through people who listen can do.

grounding: Joseph helps angry Rafiq move from a blaming channel to drain clearing and a councillor who takes the grievance seriously, finding purpose in fixing things.

passage:
For three monsoons the road from Aadhya's village to the college bus stop had turned to mud, and for three monsoons the contractor had been paid. Aadhya, twenty, had started watching one channel every night that said people in the town were laughing at villages like hers. It made her feel less stupid for being angry.
Her cousin Ankita didn't lecture. She just said, "Come with me on Sunday."
Sunday was the retired headmaster, Joshi-sir, at his verandah with three other young people. He listened to Aadhya for a full half-hour. Then he helped them write a petition to the block office with photos and dates.
The next Sunday they hauled gravel in borrowed carts and filled the worst stretch themselves. Aadhya's arms ached for two days.
She still watched the channel sometimes. But now she also read the block office notices, and had started a phone tree of twenty villagers.

qa.q: Who did Ankita take Aadhya to meet on Sunday?
qa.a: Ankita took Aadhya to the retired headmaster, Joshi-sir.

qa.q: Why did the channel appeal to Aadhya at first?
qa.a: Aadhya was angry about the ruined road and the channel made her feel less stupid for that anger, by giving her someone to blame.

qa.q: Which choice turned Aadhya's anger into something useful?
qa.a: Going with Ankita to Joshi-sir, who listened seriously and helped with a petition, and then filling the road with gravel gave her anger a purpose.

qa.q: How might Joshi-sir see young people like Aadhya?
qa.a: He seems to see their anger as real and worth hearing, which is why he listened for half an hour before helping them act.

grounding: An angry young woman in a village moves from a blaming channel to building: an elder takes her grievance seriously and she helps petition and repair the road.

passage:
Emeka had spent the winter angry. His hours at the warehouse in Johannesburg were cut, the landlord raised the rent, and the online forums he read at night all said the same thing: someone else was to blame, and they should pay.
One Saturday he walked into the community centre instead, only because his aunt made him carry soup there. Zanele, who ran the youth programme, didn't brush off his anger. "The rent thing is real," she said. "The tenants' committee meets Tuesday. Come and say it there, with facts."
He went. He met a retired bus driver, a Somali shopkeeper and two students. They argued, then drafted a letter to the council together.
By spring Emeka was fixing bicycles for kids in the centre's yard every Saturday, and reading three different news sites instead of one forum. He was still angry about the rent. But now the anger had somewhere to go that built something.

qa.q: When does the tenants' committee meet?
qa.a: The tenants' committee meets Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Emeka feel about the rent by spring?
qa.a: Emeka was still angry about the rent, but the anger felt purposeful rather than bitter, because it now went into building something.

qa.q: Which steps helped Emeka widen his circle?
qa.a: Taking the grievance to the tenants' committee, working alongside very different people, fixing bicycles for kids, and reading three news sites instead of one forum.

qa.q: How did Zanele see Emeka's anger?
qa.a: Zanele took it seriously, 'The rent thing is real', and pointed it toward the tenants' committee instead of dismissing it.

grounding: Shows an angry young man finding varied people, sources, real activities and an adult who takes his grievance seriously, and building instead of blaming.

passage:
Tenzin had been called "Chinese" and worse on the college bus four times that month. Each time he said nothing, then went back to the hostel and scrolled through pages full of rage, where people said the only answer was to hit back harder.
In November he walked into the college's student welfare office instead. Dr Sangeeta Rao listened to all four incidents, wrote down dates and bus numbers, and said, "This is not small. I'm taking it to the disciplinary committee this week." She did. Two students were called in.
Then she asked, "What would you want to build, if you could?"
Tenzin thought about it. By January he and six others, from Manipur, Kerala, Bihar and Ladakh, had started a Friday food-and-film evening in the hostel common room, open to everyone. The first week, twelve people came. The fourth week, sixty.
He unfollowed the rage pages one by one. Friday evenings were more useful.

qa.q: How many people came to the fourth Friday evening?
qa.a: The fourth week, sixty.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling after each incident on the bus?
qa.a: Tenzin felt humiliated and angry, saying nothing at the time and then scrolling rage pages in the hostel.

qa.q: Which steps turned Tenzin's anger into something useful?
qa.a: Reporting the incidents to the welfare office, being taken seriously, and building an open Friday food-and-film evening with students from many states.

qa.q: How did Dr Sangeeta Rao respond to Tenzin's complaint?
qa.a: She treated it as serious, noted dates and bus numbers, took it to the disciplinary committee that week, and asked what Tenzin would want to build.

grounding: Shows a student with a real grievance going to an adult who takes it seriously and finding purpose in building a mixed community instead of rage pages.

passage:
Dear Ms Elizabeth,
You told us in Class 12 to write to you when something big happened. This is big, in a quiet way.
Last year, after the fish in our river died and nobody from the factory or the district office answered us, I was furious. I joined groups online where people said a certain community was behind everything, and that we should "teach them a lesson". For a few weeks it felt good to have someone to hate.
Then my cousin dragged me to a meeting of the river volunteers: farmers, a retired chemistry teacher, a pastor, two engineering students. The teacher showed us how to test the water ourselves. We sent the results to the pollution board and to three newspapers, not one page.
The board has finally sent inspectors. I'm still angry. But I've left those groups, and on Sundays I test water with people who don't look or pray like me.
Aditi

qa.q: Where did the river volunteers send the water results?
qa.a: To the pollution board and to three newspapers, not one page.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel in the online groups at first?
qa.a: Aditi felt furious and helpless, and for a few weeks it felt good to have someone to hate.

qa.q: What helped Aditi find purpose beyond hating someone?
qa.a: Joining the river volunteers, learning to test the water, and sending results to the pollution board and several newspapers alongside very different people.

qa.q: How might the retired chemistry teacher see young volunteers like Aditi?
qa.a: As anger with a use; by teaching them to test the water, the teacher helped turn frustration into evidence that brought inspectors.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose anger found purpose in a mixed group of volunteers, varied sources and real action rather than online blame.

passage: You want to know how I stopped being angry all the time? I didn't, exactly. I'm Bhavna, and I'm still angry that our basti floods every monsoon while the new towers across the road stay dry. Two years ago that anger went into one page online that blamed a whole community for everything. I shared every post. It felt like a purpose. Then Francis, who runs the youth centre near the station, asked me a strange question: "What would you build, if you could?" Nobody had asked me that. He didn't say I was wrong to be angry. He said, "The flooding is real. Let's measure it." So a dozen of us, Muslim, Hindu, Christian, some who pray and some who don't, mapped every blocked drain with our phones and took it to the ward office. Half the drains were cleared last year. The page still posts. I just don't need it. I'd rather spend Saturdays with people who argue with me and still show up.

qa.q: What did Francis ask Bhavna?
qa.a: “What would you build, if you could?”

qa.q: How did sharing the page's posts make Bhavna feel at the time?
qa.a: Sharing gave Bhavna a feeling of purpose, turning anger about the flooding into blame.

qa.q: How did Francis help without dismissing the anger?
qa.a: He agreed the flooding was real and turned it into a project, mapping drains with a mixed group and taking the map to the ward office.

qa.q: How might people in the mixed group see Bhavna now?
qa.a: They probably see Bhavna as a committed teammate who argues but shows up, not as someone who blames their communities.

grounding: Shows an angry young person who finds varied friends, a real project and an adult who takes the grievance seriously, finding purpose in building rather than hating.
